The `applicationHooks` array is defined at **line 3–10** of `lib/hooks.js` and contains **6 hooks**:

| Hook | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `onRoute` | Fired when a new route is registered |
| `onRegister` | Fired when a new plugin is registered |
| `onReady` | Fired when the server is ready to start listening |
| `onListen` | Fired after the server starts listening |
| `preClose` | Fired before the server closes |
| `onClose` | Fired when the server closes |

These are distinct from the **lifecycle hooks** (lines 11–22), which are per-request hooks (`onRequest`, `preParsing`, `preValidation`, etc.). The two arrays are merged into `supportedHooks` at line 23.

Note also that in `buildHooks()` (lines 73–91), `onReady`, `onListen`, and `preClose` are **not inherited by child scopes** — they're always reset to `[]`, while the other application hooks (`onRoute`, `onRegister`) are copied via `.slice()`.

Fastify registers exactly **two** default content-type parsers out of the box. Both are set up in the `ContentTypeParser` constructor at **`lib/content-type-parser.js`, lines 37–39**:

| Content-Type | Parser | `parseAs` |
|---|---|---|
| `application/json` | `defaultJsonParser` (via `secure-json-parse`) | string (UTF-8) |
| `text/plain` | `defaultPlainTextParser` (returns body as-is) | string (UTF-8) |

**Key implementation details:**

- **`application/json`** (line 37): Uses `secureJsonParse` from the `secure-json-parse` package, guarded against prototype-poisoning and constructor-poisoning attacks. Errors on an empty body (`FST_ERR_CTP_EMPTY_JSON_BODY`) or invalid JSON (`FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_JSON_BODY`). Defined in `getDefaultJsonParser()` at line 306.

- **`text/plain`** (line 38): `defaultPlainTextParser` at line 324 — simply calls `done(null, body)`, passing the raw string body through unchanged.

Both are registered with `parseAs: 'string'` (`asString: true`), meaning the raw payload is buffered and decoded as UTF-8 before the parser function is called.

**There is no wildcard (`*`) catch-all registered by default.** If a request arrives with any other `Content-Type`, Fastify returns `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_MEDIA_TYPE` (415) unless you've added a custom parser or registered `'*'` yourself.

**Location:** `eval/repos/fastify/lib/noop-set.js`, line 3.

**What it does:** `noopSet()` is a factory that returns a no-op (stub) object that mimics the `Set` interface but does nothing:

| Method | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `[Symbol.iterator]` | Generator that yields nothing (empty iteration) |
| `add()` | No-op — silently discards the item |
| `delete()` | No-op — silently does nothing |
| `has()` | Always returns `true` |

**Why it exists:** It's used in `lib/server.js` line 139 as a drop-in replacement for a real `Set` when connection tracking isn't needed:

```js
const keepAliveConnections = !serverHasCloseAllConnections && forceCloseConnections === true
  ? new Set()
  : noopSet()
```

When `forceCloseConnections` is not `true` (or the server natively supports `closeAllConnections`), there's no need to track individual keep-alive connections. Using `noopSet()` instead of `null` means the rest of the code can call `.add()`, `.delete()`, etc. unconditionally without null-guards — it's a **null object pattern** for a `Set`.

Fastify classifies **3 HTTP methods** as `bodyless` by default, defined in [`fastify.js` line 132–137](eval/repos/fastify/fastify.js):

```js
bodyless: new Set([
  'GET',
  'HEAD',
  'TRACE'
])
```

**`GET`, `HEAD`, and `TRACE`** — requests using these methods skip body parsing entirely (`handle-request.js:29`) and will throw `FST_ERR_ROUTE_BODY_VALIDATION_SCHEMA_NOT_SUPPORTED` if a `schema.body` is defined for them (`route.js:619`).

The remaining standard methods — `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, `POST` — are in the `bodywith` set and go through the normal content-type/body-parsing pipeline.

The error code used when a request body exceeds the configured body limit is **`FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE`**, defined in [`lib/errors.js` at line 105](lib/errors.js#L105):

```js
// lib/errors.js, lines 105–108
FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE: createError(
  'FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE',
  ...,
  413,   // HTTP 413 Payload Too Large
```

It is thrown in [`lib/content-type-parser.js`](lib/content-type-parser.js) at two points:
- **Line 239**: when the incoming `Content-Length` header already exceeds the limit.
- **Line 266**: after decompression, if the decoded body length exceeds the limit (zip-bomb protection).

The error has HTTP status **413** and error code **`FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE`**.
